Sierpiński curve
The Sierpiński curve is a fractal space-filling curve introduced by Polish mathematician Wacław Sierpiński in 1912, constructed iteratively to densely fill the interior of a square while forming a continuous path of infinite length within a finite area.[1][2] Sierpiński's original construction begins with a square and proceeds through successive approximations: the first stage outlines a simple loop around the boundary, while subsequent stages divide the square into smaller subsquares (typically 16 equal parts) and replace segments with scaled, rotated copies of the previous curve, ensuring self-similarity at every level.[1][3] In the limit as iterations approach infinity, the curve passes through every point in the square's interior, embodying a paradoxical property where a one-dimensional path covers a two-dimensional region.[2] Key mathematical properties include its fractal dimension, which equals 2 (matching the plane it fills), and the enclosed area of the limiting curve, calculated as A=13(7−42)A=31​(7−42
​) for the primary variant, which is less than half the square's total area despite full coverage.[1] This curve exemplifies early 20th-century advances in topology and geometry, influencing studies in fractals, chaos theory, and applications such as antenna design and image compression due to its symmetry and space-filling efficiency.[3] Variants, like the Sierpiński arrowhead curve, adapt the construction to triangular domains, but the square-filling form remains the foundational example from Sierpiński's seminal paper "Sur une nouvelle courbe continue qui remplit toute une aire plane."[1]
Overview
Definition and Basic Characteristics
The Sierpiński curve is a fractal curve defined as a continuous surjective mapping from the unit interval [0,1][0,1] to the unit square [0,1]×[0,1][0,1]×[0,1], such that in the limit of its iterative construction, it passes through every point in the square. This space-filling property arises from an iterative process beginning with a simple closed loop around the boundary, where each subsequent approximation replaces segments with scaled and rotated copies that densely cover the square through self-similarity.[1][4] As a plane-filling curve, the Sierpiński curve exhibits a fractal structure characterized by self-similarity at every scale, meaning smaller portions of the curve resemble the whole when appropriately scaled and rotated. Its total length diverges to infinity with each iteration due to the exponential increase in the number of segments, yet it spans a finite area of 1, embodying the paradoxical nature of space-filling fractals where a one-dimensional object fills a two-dimensional region. This self-similar construction ensures the curve remains continuous and nowhere differentiable in the limit.[1][4] Visually, the Sierpiński curve initiates as a simple closed loop but rapidly evolves into an intricate triangular zigzag pattern through iterations, with folds and turns that branch into four smaller, symmetrically placed copies of the prior stage—typically rotated by 90 degrees and scaled by a factor of 1/21/2. These transformations create a dense, lattice-like filling of the unit square, resembling a crinkled or snowflake motif that becomes progressively more convoluted without intersecting itself in finite approximations.[5][4] The parametric representation of the curve relies on iterative affine transformations applied to the initial segment, such as translations, rotations, and scalings that displace midpoints and endpoints to form the zigzag motif, ensuring the overall mapping remains surjective onto the square.[1]
Historical Development
The Sierpiński curve emerged from the early 20th-century exploration of space-filling curves, a concept pioneered by Giuseppe Peano in 1890 and further developed by David Hilbert in 1891. Polish mathematician Wacław Sierpiński introduced the curve in 1912 while working at the University of Lwów, constructing it as a continuous, closed path that passes through every point in the interior of a square.[6] Sierpiński detailed this construction in his paper "Sur une nouvelle courbe continue qui remplit toute une aire plane," published in the Bulletin de l'Académie des Sciences de Cracovie (pages 462–478), where he proved the curve's continuity and surjectivity onto the unit square.[1] In this work, he demonstrated how the iterative process yields a fractal object of infinite length enclosing an area of 13(7−42)31​(7−42
​) of the square.[1] Building on this, Sierpiński published "Sur une courbe dont tout point est un point de ramification" in 1915 in the Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, describing a variant—the arrowhead curve—in which every point serves as a ramification point, exhibiting dense branching.[7] This construction connected to his contemporaneous development of the Sierpiński triangle, a fractal gasket introduced in 1915, as the arrowhead curve provides a space-filling traversal of the triangle's structure.[8] The curve gained renewed attention in the 1960s and 1970s amid the emergence of fractal theory, with Benoit Mandelbrot emphasizing its arrowhead form and self-similarity in "The Fractal Geometry of Nature" (1982), framing it as a key example of natural irregularity. During this period, connections appeared in mathematical literature to iterative variants akin to the Koch curve (introduced in 1904), influencing discussions of nowhere differentiable paths in the 1920s.[9]
Construction Methods
Iterative Geometric Construction
The iterative geometric construction of the Sierpiński curve begins with the unit square, where the zeroth approximation is a simple closed loop outlining the boundary of the square, consisting of four line segments of length 1 each, for a total length of 4.[1] In each subsequent iteration, the square is divided into 16 equal smaller subsquares arranged in a 4×4 grid. Each segment of the previous approximation is replaced by 16 scaled copies of the entire previous curve, each scaled by a factor of 1/4, and subjected to appropriate rotations and translations to fit into the subsquares while maintaining continuity of the path. The specific arrangement ensures self-similarity and that the curve traverses all subsquares in a continuous manner without self-intersection in the approximations.[3][1] The first iteration results in a more intricate closed polygon that covers the perimeter in a crinkled fashion. Higher iterations refine this pattern, with the number of segments increasing by a factor of 16 each time, leading to a total length of 4×4n4×4n at iteration n. As n approaches infinity, the curve becomes continuous and densely fills the entire unit square, passing through every point in the interior. This construction highlights the self-similar nature of the fractal, with the limiting curve having a Hausdorff dimension of 2.[1] The process can also be understood through affine transformations that map the unit square to the subsquares, combined with rotations (typically by 90 degrees or other angles as needed) to orient the subcurves correctly for seamless connection.[3]
Arrowhead Curve Variant
The arrowhead curve represents a directional variant of the Sierpiński curve construction, characterized by iterative building of triangular arrowheads that maintain a consistent pointing orientation, beginning from an initial base segment and incorporating systematic left and right turns to form pointed motifs.[10] This approach emphasizes rotational symmetry and angular precision, distinguishing it from more neutral zigzag patterns in other methods.[11] In terms of construction, each existing segment is replaced by three equal-length segments, each half the original size: proceed forward by half the length, turn 60 degrees left, proceed forward by half the length, turn 120 degrees right (equivalent to -120 degrees), and proceed forward by half the length.[11] This replacement rule, applied recursively, generates closed triangular forms at every iteration level, with the overall direction preserved for seamless concatenation of subcurves.[10] As in the general iterative geometric construction, scaling occurs uniformly by a factor of 1221​ per step, but the arrowhead variant introduces explicit 60-degree base angles to evoke triangular protrusions.[11] Visually, the curve progresses from a simple straight line at level 0, representing the base segment. At level 1, it forms a basic arrowhead triangle, consisting of three segments meeting at 60-degree angles to create a pointed equilateral motif. Subsequent levels build upon this by attaching smaller arrowheads to each segment, progressively outlining the Sierpiński gasket's structure with increasingly intricate triangular indentations before the limit curve densely traces the gasket's boundary.[10] A distinctive feature of the arrowhead curve is its analogy to dragon curves in the accumulation of turns, yet it achieves space-filling within a triangular domain, specifically the Sierpiński triangle.[12] Parametric realization via turtle graphics involves iterative moves, such as a simplified production F → F + L + F + + where F denotes forward motion, + a left turn of 60 degrees, and L a right turn adjustment, though full formalization appears in L-system contexts.[11]
Formal Representations
Lindenmayer System Formulation
The Lindenmayer system formulation provides a generative description of the Sierpiński curve using a parallel rewriting mechanism, tailored for turtle graphics interpretation. The alphabet consists of the symbols F (draw forward a unit length), + (turn left by 60°), and - (turn right by 60°), with additional non-drawing variables X and Y that are rewritten but ignored during the drawing phase.[13] The axiom is the initial string YF. The production rules are X → YF + XF + Y and Y → XF - YF - X, applied in parallel to all symbols simultaneously for each iteration.[13] To generate the curve at iteration nn, the rules are applied nn times to the axiom, producing a string that is then interpreted by a turtle starting at the origin facing along the positive x-axis: the turtle draws a line segment upon encountering F and rotates without drawing upon encountering + or -.[13][14] This deterministic context-free grammar yields the self-similar structure characteristic of the Sierpiński arrowhead curve variant. The length of the generated string grows exponentially as 3n3n, where nn is the iteration level, reflecting the tripling of symbols at each step.[13] Correspondingly, the number of F symbols, which determines the number of line segments in the curve, is exactly 3n3n.[14]
Algorithmic Implementation
The Sierpiński curve, particularly in its arrowhead variant, is commonly implemented using a recursive algorithm that builds the curve through successive subdivisions and rotations, simulating movements in a turtle graphics system. This approach generates an approximation of the curve at a specified recursion level by drawing line segments while updating position and orientation. The recursion reflects the self-similar structure, where each segment is replaced by a scaled and rotated version of the full curve pattern.[12] A typical recursive function for rendering the curve takes parameters for the current recursion level, segment length, and turning angle (usually 60 degrees). At the base case, it draws a straight line forward. For higher levels, it recursively draws three sub-curves with appropriate turns to form the arrowhead motif: one forward with negated angle, one after a left turn, and a third after another left turn with negated angle again. This produces a polyline consisting of 3n3n segments at level nn, with coordinates computed via successive 60-degree rotations.[12] The following pseudocode illustrates the core procedure:

procedure draw_curve(level, length, angle):
    if level == 0:
        forward(length)  // draw a line segment in the current direction
    else:
        draw_curve(level - 1, length / 2, -angle)
        left_turn(angle)  // rotate left by angle (60 degrees)
        draw_curve(level - 1, length / 2, angle)
        left_turn(angle)
        draw_curve(level - 1, length / 2, -angle)

To render within a unit square, the initial length is scaled inversely with the level (e.g., starting at 1/2n−11/2n−1), and the initial direction is set to 0 degrees for even levels or 60 degrees for odd levels to align the curve properly. Implementations often use libraries supporting turtle graphics or vector paths, such as the Python turtle module for interactive drawing or SVG generation for static output.[11] Efficiency is constrained by the exponential increase in segments (3n3n), limiting practical recursion depths to 10–15 levels on typical hardware, beyond which rendering becomes computationally intensive due to stack overflow risks and drawing time. For deeper approximations, non-recursive methods store the polyline as a list of points, computing positions iteratively with rotation matrices (e.g., 2D transformation matrices for 60-degree turns) to avoid recursion overhead while maintaining precision.[12]
Properties and Analysis
Fractal Dimension and Self-Similarity
The Sierpiński curve exhibits self-similarity through its iterative construction, where each stage consists of eight scaled (by a factor of 1331​), rotated, and translated copies of the previous stage, arranged to traverse the eight peripheral subsquares in a 3×3 division of the square.[1] This ensures the curve is invariant under these affine transformations and serves as an example of a self-similar space-filling curve. The fractal dimension of the Sierpiński curve is its Hausdorff dimension, which equals 2, as the limit set coincides with the full unit square. Although the construction involves eight copies at each scaling factor of 3, yielding a similarity dimension of ds=ln⁡8ln⁡3≈1.893ds​=ln3ln8​≈1.893, the dense filling of the central subsquare in the limit raises the Hausdorff dimension to 2, reflecting the curve's space-filling nature. Equivalently, the box-counting dimension approaches 2, as the number of boxes needed to cover the curve grows to fill the 2D area. Despite its topological dimension of 1 as a continuous curve, the Hausdorff dimension of 2 indicates a fractal structure that fills a 2-dimensional region while retaining one-dimensional topology. This property highlights the curve's paradoxical ability to cover the plane densely.
Space-Filling Behavior
The Sierpiński curve demonstrates space-filling behavior through its limit as a continuous surjective mapping from the unit interval [0,1][0,1] onto the unit square [0,1]×[0,1][0,1]×[0,1]. In this limit, every point in the square is attained as the image of some parameter value t∈[0,1]t∈[0,1], and the curve approaches every point arbitrarily closely with increasing iteration levels, resulting in no gaps or uncovered regions in the plane. The continuity of the limit curve holds despite its infinite length, as the sequence of polygonal approximations converges uniformly to a continuous function on the compact domain [0,1][0,1]. This uniform convergence preserves continuity, ensuring the image is a compact, connected set that coincides with the full square due to density arguments. Sierpiński established this property in his 1912 paper via a proof relying on ternary subdivision of the square, where the iterative construction ensures the curve intersects every sub-square at successively finer scales. Specifically, the square is divided into nine equal parts at each step, with the curve traversing the eight peripheral sub-squares in a prescribed order (scaled and rotated versions of the prior iteration), while the central sub-square is densely filled by later iterations, proving the curve's density in the square. Since the continuous image of a connected set is connected and the density implies the closure is the entire square, surjectivity follows.[1] Similar to the Peano curve, the Sierpiński curve fills the square topologically but introduces fractal characteristics through self-similarity; it is bijective onto its image except at a countable set of branch points, where multiple parameter values map to the same location due to the iterative folding. The parametrization exploits ternary expansions: for t∈[0,1]t∈[0,1] with ternary representation t=∑k=1∞dk3−kt=∑k=1∞​dk​3−k where dk∈{0,1,2}dk​∈{0,1,2}, the coordinates (x(t),y(t))(x(t),y(t)) are defined recursively by interpreting each digit dkdk​ to select one of the eight peripheral sub-squares and apply the corresponding affine transformation (scaling by 1/31/3, translation, and rotation by 0°, 90°, 180°, or 270° as needed for the path).
x(t)=∑k=1∞ak3−k,y(t)=∑k=1∞bk3−k,
x(t)y(t)​=k=1∑∞​ak​3−k,=k=1∑∞​bk​3−k,​ where the pairs (ak,bk)(ak​,bk​) are derived from dkdk​ via the affine maps that position and orient the segment in the chosen sub-square.
Applications
In Computer Graphics and Visualization
The Sierpiński curve, particularly its arrowhead variant, has found applications in procedural generation for computer graphics, enabling the creation of complex fractal patterns and terrains. In modeling height fields for digital elevation models (DEMs), the curve's space-filling properties facilitate efficient hierarchical triangulation, using approximately 66% of the vertices required for a naive triangle list representation (3N vertices for N triangles) while supporting multiresolution rendering. This approach constructs a Sierpiński binary triangles tree (SBT) from grid data, allowing real-time visualization of landscapes such as the Grand Canyon or Puget Sound, with post-order traversal generating continuous triangle strips for GPU rendering.[15] In software tools, the curve supports procedural texture mapping and pattern generation. For instance, MATLAB implementations leverage recursive algorithms to plot the arrowhead curve, useful for generating fractal-based textures or simulations in visualization pipelines. Similarly, vector graphics applications like Inkscape utilize L-system formulations of the curve to produce scalable patterns without rasterization artifacts, ideal for web-based visuals in SVG format. These methods draw on the curve's iterative construction to create intricate, self-similar designs for animations and static renders.[16][12] A key advantage in graphics is the curve's self-avoiding nature across finite approximations, preventing self-intersections that could complicate rendering in vector art or anti-aliased displays. This property ensures smooth, continuous paths suitable for animation trajectories, such as camera movements or particle systems that traverse fractal spaces without discontinuities. Recent developments in GPU programming, including compute shaders for adaptive tessellation, integrate the Sierpiński curve to achieve crack-free subdivision of meshes up to 31 levels, enabling real-time rendering of terrains and surfaces in interactive applications. Such techniques outperform hardware-limited tessellation by mapping leaf nodes to object space via barycentric coordinates, with execution times under 17 milliseconds on standard hardware.[17]
Practical Applications
The Sierpiński curve's symmetry and space-filling properties have been applied in antenna design, where fractal variants enable compact, multiband operation. For example, CPW-fed Sierpiński curve fractal antennas exhibit wideband performance suitable for wireless communications, and Vivaldi antennas with arrowhead curve slots are used for microwave imaging, such as stroke detection. As of 2023, these designs achieve miniaturization while maintaining efficiency across multiple frequencies.[18][19] In image compression, space-filling curves like the Sierpiński curve facilitate efficient encoding of bitmap images by traversing pixels in a locality-preserving order, reducing redundancy similar to Hilbert curves. Implementations have demonstrated compression of 16x16 bitmaps using the Sierpiński curve, aiding in fractal-based compression algorithms.[20]
In Theoretical Mathematics and Modeling
The Sierpiński curve, particularly its arrowhead variant, serves as a model in dynamical systems due to its self-similar structure, which parallels chaotic attractors and Julia sets in complex dynamics. In rational maps of the form fλ(z)=zn+λ/znfλ​(z)=zn+λ/zn, the Julia sets often exhibit Sierpiński curve topology, forming connected, nowhere dense continua that embed every plane continuum homeomorphically. This self-similarity links the curve to iterated function systems (IFS), where the limit set arises from contractive mappings, analogous to how the Sierpiński gasket is generated by three affine transformations, though the curve itself employs L-systems for iterative construction.[21][11] In measure theory, the Sierpiński curve exemplifies continuous nowhere-differentiable functions, as its parametrization from the unit interval to the plane lacks a derivative at any point, proven through analysis of polygonal approximations showing unbounded variation.[22] In the 2020s, research on quantum walks over fractal graphs, such as the Sierpiński gasket approximating the arrowhead variant's triangular support, reveals localization phenomena and slowed spreading dynamics, contrasting classical diffusion on Euclidean lattices. A unique analytical counterexample provided by the curve is a continuous path that is non-rectifiable, possessing infinite arc length despite bounded image, due to its Hausdorff dimension exceeding 1. Its space-filling behavior underpins these applications by enabling dense embeddings in low-dimensional domains.[23][1]

Peano curve
The Peano curve is a continuous surjective mapping from the unit interval [0,1][0,1] onto the unit square [0,1]×[0,1][0,1]×[0,1], representing the first known example of a space-filling curve that densely fills a two-dimensional region without gaps or discontinuities in the limit.[1] Introduced by Italian mathematician Giuseppe Peano in 1890, it provides a counterexample to intuitive assumptions about dimensional invariance under continuous functions, showing how a one-dimensional line can cover an entire plane area.[2] The construction of the Peano curve proceeds iteratively, starting with a basic polyline that traverses nine equal subsquares of the unit square in a specific order, such as an S-shaped path.[3] In each subsequent iteration, every line segment is replaced by a scaled and possibly rotated or reflected version of the full previous curve, with the process based on ternary (base-3) representations of points in the interval to ensure surjectivity.[3] The limiting curve as iterations approach infinity is continuous everywhere but nowhere differentiable, satisfying a Hölder condition with exponent α=1/2α=1/2, and possesses a Hausdorff dimension of 2, matching that of the square it fills.[4] Peano curves hold significant theoretical importance in topology and fractal geometry, illustrating the non-intuitive properties of continuous mappings between spaces of different dimensions and influencing subsequent constructions like the Hilbert curve.[5] In applied mathematics and computing, variants of the Peano curve are utilized for multidimensional database indexing to preserve spatial locality, dimension reduction in data processing, and optimizing parallel algorithms such as cache-oblivious matrix multiplication.[5][4] They also appear in image processing for halftone patterns that maintain smooth gradients and crisp details, and in signal coverage models to minimize memory usage.[6][4]
History and Context
Origins and Development
In the late 19th century, mathematical debates on dimension, continuity, and the nature of infinite sets intensified, particularly following Georg Cantor's demonstrations that the real numbers form an uncountable set and that the unit interval and unit square have the same cardinality. These ideas raised questions about whether a continuous function could map a one-dimensional line onto a two-dimensional plane, challenging intuitive geometric notions. Italian mathematician Giuseppe Peano addressed this in 1890 by constructing the first explicit example of such a mapping, a continuous surjection from the unit interval to the unit square. Peano's seminal paper, titled Sur une courbe, qui remplit toute une aire plane, was published in Mathematische Annalen, volume 36, pages 157–160.[7] In it, he described an iterative process using ternary expansions to define the curve, demonstrating that it fills the entire plane area without gaps, though his presentation lacked detailed illustrations and relied on analytical description. This work directly responded to the paradoxes emerging from Cantor's set theory, illustrating how a path of dimension 1 could cover a region of dimension 2. One year later, German mathematician David Hilbert provided a more geometrically intuitive variant in his 1891 paper Über die stetige Abbildung einer Linie auf ein Flächenstück, published in Mathematische Annalen, volume 38, pages 459–460. Hilbert's construction used a sequence of polygonal approximations that preserved locality better than Peano's, making it easier to visualize and influencing subsequent developments in fractal geometry. In 1904, French mathematician Henri Lebesgue further analyzed space-filling curves in his book Leçons sur l'intégration et la recherche des fonctions primitives, where he confirmed their pathological properties, such as nowhere differentiability, while integrating them into the foundations of measure theory.[8]
Mathematical Significance
The Peano curve provides a foundational example in topology by demonstrating the existence of a continuous surjective function from the one-dimensional unit interval [0,1][0,1] onto the two-dimensional unit square [0,1]2[0,1]2. This space-filling property reveals that a continuous image of a lower-dimensional space can completely cover a higher-dimensional region, directly challenging the pre-20th-century intuition that dimension remains invariant under continuous mappings. Such a construction was counterintuitive at the time, as it suggested that topological properties alone do not preclude "filling" higher dimensions without introducing discontinuities or gaps.[9][10] This phenomenon aligns with the set-theoretic fact that [0,1][0,1] and [0,1]2[0,1]2 possess the same cardinality, known as the cardinality of the continuum, denoted 2ℵ02ℵ0​. While bijections exist between these sets at the level of pure sets, the Peano curve achieves a continuous surjection, offering a topological analogue to this equicardinality and demonstrating that the intervals are equidecomposable in a continuous sense. However, the curve is highly non-injective, with most points in the square having uncountably many preimages, reflecting the limitations imposed by topological structure beyond mere cardinality.[11][9] The absence of a continuous bijection between [0,1][0,1] and [0,1]2[0,1]2 follows from the invariance of dimension theorem, which asserts that Euclidean spaces of differing dimensions are not homeomorphic; a homeomorphism would require both surjectivity and injectivity in a continuous manner. The Peano curve exemplifies this by being surjective yet nowhere injective, as its self-intersections prevent it from establishing a one-to-one correspondence, thereby illustrating the theorem's role in distinguishing dimensional topologies.[12] The Peano curve's insights spurred advancements in algebraic topology, including L. E. J. Brouwer's fixed-point theorem and invariance of domain theorem, by necessitating rigorous definitions of dimension to resolve paradoxes arising from space-filling constructions. In measure theory, it highlights non-intuitive aspects of Lebesgue measure, where the curve's image attains full two-dimensional measure despite its one-dimensional parametrization, demonstrating how continuous maps can transform measures in singular ways that defy geometric expectations.[10][13]
Definition and Properties
Formal Definition
The Peano curve is formally defined as a continuous surjective function f:[0,1]→[0,1]×[0,1]f:[0,1]→[0,1]×[0,1], such that the image of the unit interval under ff covers the entire unit square, with every point in the square attained by at least one value in the interval. This mapping, introduced by Giuseppe Peano in 1890, satisfies the topological conditions of the Hahn-Mazurkiewicz theorem, which (in its standard form) characterizes compact, connected, and locally connected metric spaces as continuous images of the unit interval, though Peano's construction predates the theorem. One explicit representation of the Peano curve f(t)=(x(t),y(t))f(t)=(x(t),y(t)) for t∈[0,1]t∈[0,1] relies on the ternary (base-3) expansion of t=∑k=1∞tk3−kt=∑k=1∞​tk​3−k, where each digit tk∈{0,1,2}tk​∈{0,1,2}. The coordinate functions are then given by

x(t)=j=1∑∞​xj​3−j,y(t)=j=1∑∞​yj​3−j, where the ternary digits xjxj​ and yjyj​ (each in {0, 1, 2}) are derived from the tktk​ via a specific encoding that ensures the curve fills the square. Define the transformation k(d)=2−dk(d)=2−d for d∈{0,1,2}d∈{0,1,2}, and let kvkv​ denote the vv-th iterate of kk (with k0(d)=dk0​(d)=d). The digits are assigned as follows: the first digit of x(t)x(t) is x1=t1x1​=t1​, the first digit of y(t)y(t) is y1=kt1(t2)y1​=kt1​​(t2​), and subsequent digits alternate in grouping, with indices depending on partial sums of the tktk​ to map into the appropriate subquadrants (e.g., adjusting for even and odd positions to connect across the nine subsquares of a ternary grid).[3] This functional form arises as the uniform limit of a sequence of polygonal approximations fn:[0,1]→[0,1]×[0,1]fn​:[0,1]→[0,1]×[0,1], where each fnfn​ is a continuous piecewise linear curve consisting of 9n9n line segments of length 3−n3−n, subdividing the unit square into a 3n×3n3n×3n grid and traversing it in a space-filling manner; convergence to ff is uniform by the Weierstrass M-test applied to the series representations of x(t)x(t) and y(t)y(t).
Continuity and Surjectivity
The Peano curve is constructed as the pointwise limit f=lim⁡n→∞fnf=limn→∞​fn​ of a sequence of continuous polygonal paths fn:[0,1]→[0,1]2fn​:[0,1]→[0,1]2, where each fnfn​ connects the centers of 9n9n smaller squares tiling the unit square via piecewise linear segments.[14] Since the sequence {fn}{fn​} converges uniformly to ff—with sup⁡x∈[0,1]∥fn(x)−fm(x)∥<2⋅3−min⁡(n,m)supx∈[0,1]​∥fn​(x)−fm​(x)∥<2
​⋅3−min(n,m) for n,mn,m sufficiently large—the uniform limit theorem for functions on compact metric spaces guarantees that ff is continuous.[14] To establish surjectivity, observe that each fnfn​ passes through the centers of all 9n9n subsquares of side length 3−n3−n, so the image of fnfn​ is 22⋅3−n22
​​⋅3−n-dense in [0,1]2[0,1]2. The uniform convergence of {fn}{fn​} to ff implies that the image of ff contains all limit points of these dense approximations. Since the image of ff is compact (as the continuous image of the compact set [0,1][0,1]) and thus closed, and it contains a dense subset of [0,1]2[0,1]2, it must equal the entire unit square, proving ff is surjective.[14] The Peano curve is not injective: for most points in [0,1]2[0,1]2, there are multiple preimages under ff, leading to self-intersections along the curve. Specifically, a continuous surjective map from the one-dimensional interval [0,1][0,1] to the two-dimensional square [0,1]2[0,1]2 cannot be injective, as injectivity would imply a homeomorphism by the invariance of domain theorem, which is impossible due to differing topological dimensions. The density of the curve's image in [0,1]2[0,1]2 ensures that these self-intersections occur infinitely often, as the iterative approximations intersect themselves at increasingly finer scales throughout the square.[14] Pathologically, the Peano curve is nowhere differentiable, meaning its coordinate functions lack a derivative at any point in [0,1][0,1]; this was first proved by E. H. Moore in 1900 using properties of the curve's ternary expansion-based parametrization.[13] Moreover, while a partial inverse selecting one preimage for points with multiple preimages can be defined, it is discontinuous everywhere, reflecting the failure of ff to induce a continuous bijection.[14]
Construction Methods
Iterative Geometric Construction
The iterative geometric construction of the Peano curve begins by dividing the unit square into nine equal subsquares of size 13×1331​×31​. The first approximation is an S-shaped polyline consisting of eight line segments of length 1331​ that connects the centers of these subsquares in a serpentine order, visiting all nine subsquares continuously.[3] For higher iterations, each straight segment from the prior approximation is replaced by a scaled (by 1331​), rotated, or reflected copy of the full previous curve, with the unit square divided into 3n×3n3n×3n subsquares; the path traverses these via recursive self-similar placement in the nine level-(n-1) blocks, ensuring continuity.[15][16] The resulting nth approximation, denoted PnPn​, consists of 8×9n−18×9n−1 line segments, each of length 3−n3−n, yielding a total length of 8×3n−28×3n−2, which increases exponentially with nn; nevertheless, the sequence {Pn}{Pn​} converges uniformly to the continuous limit curve due to the decreasing scale of the subsquares and the dense coverage achieved at each step.[17][18] Visual representations of the first few iterations illustrate this process: the first iteration is the S-shaped path spanning all nine subsquares; subsequent steps reveal a progressively intricate, self-similar pattern that weaves through finer grids, emphasizing the curve's ability to fill the entire unit square without gaps or overlaps in the infinite limit.[3][16]
L-System Generation
The Peano curve can be generated using a Lindenmayer system (L-system), which employs parallel string rewriting to model its self-similar, space-filling properties. The alphabet consists of drawing symbols F (move forward while drawing a line segment), + (turn left by 90 degrees), and - (turn right by 90 degrees), along with non-drawing symbols X and Y that guide the rewriting process but are ignored during graphical interpretation. The axiom is the string X, and the production rules are X → XFYFX+F+YFXFY−F−XFYFX and Y → YFXFY−F−XFYFX+F+YFXFY.[18] To construct the curve, the rules are applied iteratively in parallel to every symbol in the current string for n steps, producing a longer string at each iteration. This string is then interpreted via turtle graphics: starting from an initial position and orientation, F advances the turtle by a fixed step length while drawing, + and - rotate the turtle by 90 degrees without drawing (with the convention that + is a left turn and - a right turn in this context), and X and Y are skipped. At iteration n, the step length is scaled by a factor of 1/3 relative to the previous level to ensure the path remains bounded within the unit square, resulting in 8 \times 9^{n-1} line segments that increasingly densely approximate the space-filling limit.[18][19] This L-system approach highlights the fractal, self-similar nature of the Peano curve, where each iteration embeds nine scaled copies of the previous path connected by turns, formalizing the recursive subdivision of the square into nine subsquares. It enables straightforward computational generation of the curve for arbitrary n, making it ideal for software implementations in graphics and simulation, as the string rewriting is efficient and the resulting path directly translatable to vector coordinates.[18] Variations in the production rules allow for different routings of the Peano curve while preserving its space-filling essence. For instance, adjusted sequences of + and - can modify the order in which subsquares are traversed, potentially reducing self-intersections in finite approximations or adapting the curve for specific grid traversals, such as in self-avoiding paths for computational mapping.[19]
Variants and Extensions
Notable Variants
One prominent variant of the Peano curve is the Hilbert curve, introduced by David Hilbert in 1891 as a continuous surjective mapping from the unit interval to the unit square that avoids self-intersections in its finite approximations.[20] Unlike the original Peano curve, which exhibits self-intersections, the Hilbert curve is constructed iteratively by dividing the square into four quadrants and connecting smaller copies of the curve with 90-degree turns, resulting in a non-crossing path that better preserves locality—meaning points close in the one-dimensional parameter remain spatially proximate in the two-dimensional embedding. This locality property arises from its recursive structure, often generated using an L-system.[21] The Sierpinski curve, also known as the arrowhead curve, was described by Wacław Sierpiński in 1912 as a solution to certain functional equations, providing a continuous surjection from the unit interval onto the Sierpinski triangle gasket—a self-similar fractal set—rather than a full square. It is constructed iteratively by replacing each line segment with an arrowhead shape—two segments at 60-degree angles—yielding a self-similar fractal whose image is the Sierpinski gasket in the limit.[22] This variant employs an order-2 L-system for generation, with rules like F → G-F-G and G → F+G+F (angle 60°), emphasizing its gasket domain and rotational symmetry, which distinguishes it from square-filling Peano derivatives.[22] Another notable variant is the Moore curve, proposed by E. H. Moore in 1900, which extends the Hilbert construction into a closed loop by combining four rotated Hilbert subcurves such that endpoints coincide. It achieves bijectivity on the dyadic grid points of the square (one-to-one correspondence in finite approximations) while remaining surjective in the continuous limit, differing from the Peano and Hilbert curves by incorporating even-odd parity routings in quadrant traversals to ensure closure without overlaps.
Variant	Self-Intersection	Domain Filled	Locality Preservation	Computational Complexity (Order n)
Peano	Yes	Square	Moderate	O(9^n) points
Hilbert	No	Square	High	O(4^n) points
Sierpinski	Yes	Sierpinski gasket	Moderate	O(3^n) points
Moore	No (closed)	Square	High	O(4^n) points
These differences highlight trade-offs in the variants: Hilbert and Moore prioritize non-intersection and locality for applications like data indexing, while Sierpinski's gasket focus suits fractal geometry studies.
Generalizations to Higher Dimensions
The Peano curve generalizes to n-dimensional spaces for n ≥ 2 as a continuous surjective map f:[0,1]→[0,1]nf:[0,1]→[0,1]n, often constructed by extending the base-3 ternary expansion of a parameter t ∈ [0,1] to n-tuples of digits from {0,1,2}, where each digit sequence determines the coordinates via affine transformations that map subintervals to sub-hypercubes. This approach, formalized by Kôno, ensures the curve fills the unit hypercube while maintaining continuity through self-similar subdivisions, with each coordinate function being 1/n-Hölder continuous but nowhere differentiable for q > 1/n.[23] The resulting curve is uniformly distributed and has graphs with Hausdorff dimension 2 - 1/n, preserving key pathological properties of the original 2D version. A prominent variant in higher dimensions is the n-dimensional Hilbert curve, which iteratively divides the unit hypercube into 2^n smaller hypercubes and traverses them in a locality-preserving order using Gray codes and rotations to connect adjacent subcubes continuously.[24] This construction, generalizing Hilbert's 1891 2D design, ensures that nearby points in the 1D parameter map to nearby points in the nD space, making it suitable for multi-dimensional data indexing and traversal while filling the hypercube surjectively in the limit. In 3D, for instance, over 1500 distinct structural variants exist, each preserving the curve's bijective approximation properties up to finite resolutions.[24] Fractal generalizations extend Peano-like curves to non-simply connected sets, such as the Sierpinski gasket in 2D or the Menger sponge in 3D, where iterative removals create porous attractors that the curve densely fills via adapted subdivisions. On the Sierpinski gasket, the Sierpinski curve—a symmetric space-filling variant—uses triangular rep-tiles to map [0,1] surjectively onto the gasket, achieving a Hausdorff dimension of log(3)/log(2) ≈ 1.585 while maintaining continuity. Similarly, for the Menger sponge, Peano-inspired curves traverse the sponge's cubic lattice by avoiding removed central subcubes, resulting in a topologically one-dimensional continuum that fills the fractal set of dimension log(20)/log(3) ≈ 2.727 without locally separating points.[25] In abstract settings like metric spaces or compact connected manifolds, Peano curve principles yield continuous surjections from [0,1] to higher-dimensional targets by embedding them as the image of a compact subset via iterative approximations. These generalizations demonstrate that space-filling behavior persists in non-Euclidean geometries, provided the target admits a metric compatible with its topology, enabling surjective fillings without injectivity.
Applications
Theoretical Implications
The Peano curve occupies a central position in fractal geometry, serving as a foundational example of a space-filling curve whose image has Hausdorff dimension 2. This property reveals how a topologically one-dimensional object can exhibit a two-dimensional Hausdorff measure, challenging classical notions of dimension and measure in Euclidean spaces. By filling the unit square completely while remaining continuous, the curve demonstrates the capacity of fractal sets to blur the boundaries between dimensions, influencing subsequent developments in the study of self-similar structures and irregular sets.[26] The self-intersecting character of the Peano curve underscores limitations in classical topological theorems, particularly the Jordan curve theorem, which applies only to simple closed curves. Unlike a simple Jordan curve that separates the plane into distinct interior and exterior regions, the Peano curve's dense self-intersections result in an image that encompasses the entire square, rendering the complement empty and eliminating any well-defined "inside" or "outside." This pathological behavior highlights the necessity of the non-self-intersection condition in the Jordan theorem and motivates deeper investigations into the topology of non-injective mappings.[14] In dynamical systems, the Peano curve facilitates explorations of ergodic theory and symbolic dynamics, often via itinerary maps that encode the curve's path through symbolic sequences. Its construction aligns naturally with self-similar groups, allowing translations of geometric iterations into algebraic and symbolic frameworks that model complex orbit behaviors. This connection enables the analysis of invariant measures and mixing properties in systems where continuous surjections mimic the curve's filling action.[27] Post-2000 advancements have leveraged Peano curves in proving density of orbits within chaotic systems, particularly through iterations of expanding maps. For instance, Daniel Meyer's work constructs invariant Peano curves for expanding Thurston maps, thereby enhancing understanding of hyperbolic dynamics and stochastic stability. These applications underscore the curve's enduring role in bridging geometry and chaos theory.[28]
Computational Uses
Peano curves are employed in data structures to order elements in multi-dimensional arrays, enhancing cache locality by preserving spatial proximity during linear traversals. This approach maps higher-dimensional data to one-dimensional sequences, reducing cache misses in operations on large datasets such as images or matrices. For instance, in image processing, Peano curve orderings outperform Z-order curves by providing better clustering of nearby pixels, which minimizes random memory accesses during filtering or compression tasks.[29][30] In matrix operations, block-recursive algorithms using Peano curve-based element ordering achieve cache-oblivious performance, adapting to any cache hierarchy without prior knowledge of cache sizes. These algorithms process submatrices in a locality-preserving manner, significantly lowering cache misses for tasks like matrix multiplication and LU decomposition compared to row-major or column-major orderings.[29] In computer graphics and rendering, Peano curves generate space-filling paths that facilitate efficient texture mapping and antialiasing by traversing pixel grids in a continuous order. This locality preservation ensures smoother interpolation across adjacent texels, reducing artifacts in rendered images. A common iterative method for generating such curves up to level n=7n=7 (yielding 37=218737=2187 segments) uses recursive subdivision: start with a base curve at level 1 (a sideways "2" shape spanning the unit square), then replace each segment with a scaled copy of the level-n−1n−1 curve, oriented and connected to form nine sub-squares. The following pseudocode illustrates this recursive generation, outputting line segments as coordinates:

function generate_peano(level n, position (x, y), orientation dir, scale s):
    if n == 0:
        return single segment from (x, y) to (x + s, y + s) based on dir
    else:
        sub_scale = s / 3
        for i in 0 to 8:  // nine sub-curves
            sub_x = x + (i % 3) * sub_scale
            sub_y = y + floor(i / 3) * sub_scale
            sub_dir = determine_orientation(i, dir)  // e.g., rotate/flip based on i
            generate_peano(n-1, (sub_x, sub_y), sub_dir, sub_scale)
            // Connect sub-curves sequentially

This algorithm, limited to n≤7n≤7 for practical computation, is detailed in early graphics literature for curve approximation.[31] In scientific computing, Peano curves enable efficient grid traversals for simulations on adaptive Cartesian meshes, such as those in finite element methods for solving partial differential equations. The Peano software framework implements automaton-based traversals tied to space-filling curve orderings, linearizing 2D and 3D data to reduce memory access overhead by exploiting data locality across levels. This results in high cache hit rates and scalable parallel performance on shared or distributed systems, with applications in computational fluid dynamics where single-pass algorithms handle mesh partitioning and interpolation. For example, Peano-Hilbert orderings in CFD yield up to 96% overlap in multigrid transfers, minimizing communication costs.[32][33][34] In geographic information systems (GIS), variants of Peano curves such as Peano-Hilbert are used for sequencing spatial tiles via bit-interleaving of coordinates, enabling efficient range queries on map databases. This preserves locality for overlapping regions, reducing query times to O(log N) for rectangular windows. In machine learning, Peano-like space-filling curves linearize high-dimensional data into 1D sequences for tasks like image classification and point cloud processing, improving autocorrelation in embeddings and compression ratios in computer vision models. Data-adaptive variants, optimized via graph neural networks, enhance feature extraction by modeling curves as Hamiltonian paths on grids.[35][36]

Chaos game
The chaos game is a probabilistic algorithm for generating fractals, introduced by mathematician Michael Barnsley in his 1988 book Fractals Everywhere, which iteratively constructs self-similar patterns by starting from an arbitrary point and repeatedly moving it a fixed fraction (typically 1/2) of the distance toward one of several predefined target points chosen at random, often the vertices of a polygon, resulting in approximations of attractors from iterated function systems (IFS).[1][2] In its simplest form, applied to an equilateral triangle with vertices labeled A, B, and C, the algorithm begins with a seed point inside the triangle and, for each iteration, selects one vertex uniformly at random and places the next point midway between the current point and the chosen vertex; after sufficiently many iterations (discarding the initial few to avoid transient effects), the plotted points densely fill the Sierpinski triangle, a classic fractal with Hausdorff dimension approximately 1.585, demonstrating how deterministic chaos can emerge from random choices within contractive mappings.[3][1] This process generalizes to higher-sided regular polygons or arbitrary IFS, where affine transformations replace vertex selections, enabling the creation of more complex structures like the Barnsley fern—a realistic fern-like fractal attractor defined by four contractive maps with probabilities 0.01, 0.85, 0.07, and 0.07, respectively, which converges to a fixed point under repeated application due to the system's contraction factor being less than 1.[4][1] The chaos game's significance lies in its illustration of Barnsley's IFS theory, where the attractor is the unique fixed point of the Hutchinson operator on compact sets, provably reached almost surely under mild conditions on the transformations' contractivity, as later formalized in works like Barnsley and Vince's analysis of general IFS on metric spaces.[5] It has applications in computer graphics, image compression, and modeling natural phenomena, highlighting the interplay between randomness and order in dynamical systems, though convergence speed varies with parameters like the contraction ratio r and the number of iterations needed to approximate the attractor accurately.[1][2]
Fundamentals
Definition and History
The chaos game is a probabilistic algorithm used to visualize and generate approximations of fractal attractors defined by iterated function systems (IFS). Fractals are geometric objects that exhibit self-similarity at every scale, often arising as the fixed points of repeated transformations, a concept popularized by Benoit Mandelbrot in his 1975 work Fractals: Form, Chance, and Dimension. An IFS consists of a finite set of contractive affine transformations on a metric space, where the attractor is the unique compact set invariant under the union of these maps, satisfying the Hutchinson equation A=⋃i=1Nfi(A)A=⋃i=1N​fi​(A), with contraction ensuring convergence to this fixed point. In the chaos game, the process begins with an arbitrary initial point in the plane and iteratively selects a transformation from the IFS at random (typically with equal probability) to update the point's position, plotting each new point to form a dense approximation of the attractor after sufficient iterations. This method leverages chaotic dynamics to produce the fractal structure efficiently on a computer, bypassing explicit construction of the self-similar set. The resulting point cloud converges almost surely to the IFS attractor regardless of the starting point, highlighting the robustness of the approach.[6] The chaos game was introduced by Michael Barnsley and Alan Sloan in their 1988 article in BYTE magazine, where it was presented as a tool for fractal image compression and generation, enabling high compression ratios by modeling images as IFS attractors. Barnsley further formalized and expanded on the technique in his 1988 book Fractals Everywhere, establishing it as a key visualization method for IFS theory. This development built on earlier work in dynamical systems. Barnsley and Sloan founded Iterated Systems, Inc. in 1987 to commercialize IFS-based technologies.[6][7][8] A simple pseudocode example for the basic chaos game setup, using a triangular IFS (e.g., for the Sierpinski triangle), illustrates the core iteration without specific parameters:

Choose initial point P(0) arbitrarily in the [plane](/page/Plane).
For n = 1 to N (large N):
    Select k randomly from {1, 2, 3} with equal probability.
    Set P(n) = (P(n-1) + V_k) / 2, where V_1, V_2, V_3 are the triangle vertices.
    Plot P(n) (discard first few points if needed).

This generates points that approximate the attractor through repeated midpoint contractions toward randomly chosen vertices.[6]
Basic Algorithm
The chaos game is a randomized iterative algorithm for approximating the attractor of an iterated function system (IFS), originally described by Michael Barnsley in his 1988 textbook Fractals Everywhere.[9] The procedure generates a sequence of points that, under appropriate conditions, densely fill the fractal attractor after many iterations.[1] The basic algorithm proceeds in the following steps:

    Select an initial point P0P0​ at an arbitrary location in the plane.[1]
    Choose nn fixed points V1,V2,…,VnV1​,V2​,…,Vn​, which serve as the vertices of a polygon or the fixed points of an IFS.[9]
    For each iteration k=1k=1 to NN, where NN is a large number:
        Randomly select one of the points ViVi​ (for i=1i=1 to nn) with equal probability using a pseudorandom number generator.
        Compute the next point PkPk​ via the affine transformation
        Pk=(1−r)Pk−1+rVi,
        Pk​=(1−r)Pk−1​+rVi​, where rr (with 0<r<10<r<1) is the contraction ratio.
        Plot or record the point PkPk​.[1][9]

A key property of the algorithm is its convergence: after a sufficient number of iterations (typically 10,000 or more), the plotted points densely approximate the attractor of the IFS, regardless of the initial point P0P0​.[1] To avoid distortions from transient behavior, the first few hundred points are often discarded before visualization. In implementation, pseudorandom selection ensures the probabilistic nature of the process, and efficient plotting techniques—such as buffering points before rendering—are essential for handling large NN (e.g., millions) to produce clear visualizations without performance bottlenecks.[1]
Core Parameters
Contraction Ratio r
In the chaos game, the contraction ratio rr is a key parameter that specifies the scaling factor in the affine transformations applied to generate the fractal attractor. It represents the fixed weight assigned to the randomly selected vertex in each iteration's position update, given by Pk=(1−r)Pk−1+rViPk​=(1−r)Pk−1​+rVi​, where ViVi​ is one of the predefined vertices chosen with equal probability and 0<r<10<r<1 ensures the mappings are contractive, promoting convergence to the unique attractor of the underlying iterated function system (IFS).[10] This range for rr is essential, as it aligns with the requirements for hyperbolic IFSs, where the transformations reduce distances between points.[11] The choice of rr significantly influences the visual and dynamical properties of the generated plot. For r=0.5r=0.5, the contraction is balanced, enabling points to efficiently explore and densely fill the attractor, as seen in classic examples like the Sierpinski triangle. Smaller values of rr, such as 0.2, lead to slower convergence because the influence of the previous position dominates (1−r1−r is larger), resulting in sparser distributions where points inch gradually toward the structure. Conversely, as rr approaches 1, the selected vertex exerts nearly full control, causing iterations to "stick" close to the vertices and producing plots with reduced interior density and more pronounced clustering at the boundaries.[11][10] Mathematically, rr determines the Lipschitz constant of the IFS maps, bounding the expansion of distances by ∥fi(x)−fi(y)∥≤r∥x−y∥∥fi​(x)−fi​(y)∥≤r∥x−y∥ for all maps fifi​. With max⁡iri<1maxi​ri​<1 (often uniform rr), the associated Markov operator on the space of probability measures is a contraction mapping in the Hutchinson metric, guaranteeing a unique invariant measure supported on the attractor by the contraction mapping theorem.[10] This framework ensures that the chaos game's random iterations approximate the attractor arbitrarily closely after sufficiently many steps, with the rate governed by rr.[12] To illustrate rr's dynamical effect, consider the expected position update under uniform vertex selection. Let PkPk​ denote the position after kk iterations, and assume the vertices V1,…,VnV1​,…,Vn​ are equally likely with centroid Vˉ=1n∑i=1nViVˉ=n1​∑i=1n​Vi​. Taking expectations yields
E[Pk]=(1−r)E[Pk−1]+rE[Vi]=(1−r)E[Pk−1]+rVˉ,
E[Pk​]=(1−r)E[Pk−1​]+rE[Vi​]=(1−r)E[Pk−1​]+rVˉ, since E[Vi]=VˉE[Vi​]=Vˉ. This is a linear recurrence relation, solved iteratively as E[Pk]=(1−r)k(E[P0]−Vˉ)+VˉE[Pk​]=(1−r)k(E[P0​]−Vˉ)+Vˉ. The term (1−r)k(1−r)k decays exponentially to 0 for r>0r>0, demonstrating geometric convergence of the mean position to the centroid at rate 1−r1−r; smaller rr slows this process, consistent with the sparser plots observed. This derivation highlights how rr controls the bias toward the vertices' average while the stochastic selection fills the full attractor.[10]
Jump Size and Probability
In the chaos game algorithm, the selection of vertices (or more generally, transformations in an iterated function system) follows a probabilistic model where each of the nn vertices is chosen uniformly at random with probability 1/n1/n. This uniform distribution ensures that the iterative process explores the attractor in a balanced manner, leading to a dense approximation of the fractal set after sufficiently many iterations. For weighted iterated function systems, non-uniform probabilities can be assigned to each transformation, allowing for biased sampling that emphasizes certain substructures within the attractor.[13] The jump size refers to the displacement between consecutive points in the sequence, defined as ∥Pk−Pk−1∥=r∥Vσk−Pk−1∥∥Pk​−Pk−1​∥=r∥Vσk​​−Pk−1​∥, where VσkVσk​​ is the randomly selected vertex, rr is the contraction ratio, and Pk−1Pk−1​ is the previous point. This formulation positions the new point PkPk​ at a fractional distance rr along the line segment from Pk−1Pk−1​ to VσkVσk​​, effectively contracting the step toward the vertex by the factor rr. In the standard implementation with r=0.5r=0.5, each jump moves halfway to the selected vertex, which, combined with the probabilistic selection, generates a dense filling of the fractal attractor.[14] The interplay between jump size and probability profoundly affects the resulting point cloud. With uniform probabilities and r=0.5r=0.5, the process yields a uniform density across the attractor, approximating its Hausdorff measure. Non-uniform probabilities, however, concentrate point density in regions corresponding to higher-probability transformations, enabling the visualization of measures supported on the fractal. For instance, in the case of an equilateral triangle with n=3n=3 vertices, selecting each with equal probability 1/31/3 and r=0.5r=0.5 produces the Sierpinski triangle, where points densely cover the attractor uniformly after thousands of iterations.[13]

The chaos game provides a straightforward method to generate the Sierpinski triangle, a canonical fractal attractor, by applying the algorithm to three vertices forming an equilateral triangle with contraction ratio r=0.5r=0.5. As iterations continue, points fill smaller sub-triangles at the corners and midpoints, with densities building outward from vertices to reveal the gasket's porous structure after approximately 10,000 points.[15] Michael Barnsley's 1988 demonstration of the chaos game in Fractals Everywhere popularized this iterative technique for visualizing the Sierpinski triangle, highlighting its efficiency in approximating IFS attractors without explicit geometric construction.[16] The underlying IFS consists of the following affine transformations, each contracting by 0.5 toward one vertex:

Other Iterated Function Systems
The chaos game extends beyond the simple triangular setup to arbitrary iterated function systems (IFS), allowing the generation of diverse self-similar fractals through random application of multiple contractive transformations. An IFS consists of a finite collection of contractive mappings {Wi}i=1N{Wi​}i=1N​ on a complete metric space, with the unique nonempty compact attractor HH satisfying the Hutchinson equation
H=⋃i=1NWi(H).
H=i=1⋃N​Wi​(H). The chaos game approximates this attractor by initializing a point (often an arbitrary one or a fixed point of the system) and iteratively replacing it with Wi(P)Wi​(P), where PP is the current point and ii is selected randomly according to contractivity conditions that ensure convergence in distribution to the invariant measure on HH.[9][14] Adaptations for general IFS replace the triangular vertices with a suitable initial set, such as the fixed points of the mappings or an approximation of the attractor, and incorporate non-uniform selection probabilities to capture asymmetric structures. For instance, in asymmetric fractals like Barnsley's fern, probabilities are tuned to reflect structural dominance, such as assigning 0.01 to the stem transformation and 0.85 to the main frond transformation, ensuring rare but critical features emerge amid frequent leaf iterations.[9] Barnsley's fern exemplifies this approach using four affine mappings in the plane: one for the thin, vertical stem with minimal contraction and slight rotation; one for the large main frond with scaling approximately 0.85; two for the successively smaller leaflets with scalings approximately 0.4 and rotations to mimic branching; and one for the base with adjusted translation and rotation to position the structure.[9][4] The Koch curve, in contrast, employs four mappings on the endpoints of an initial line segment, each contracting by a factor of 1/31/3 while applying translations and ±60∘±60∘ rotations to two intermediate vertices, producing the iterative "bumps" characteristic of this boundary fractal. In one dimension, the Cantor set arises from two uniform mappings on the interval [0,1]: W1(x)=x/3W1​(x)=x/3 and W2(x)=(x+2)/3W2​(x)=(x+2)/3, iteratively removing middle thirds to form a dust-like attractor of measure zero.[9][17] Generating and visualizing these IFS attractors via the chaos game introduces challenges, especially in higher dimensions where direct plotting requires dimensionality reduction techniques like projections, and in distinguishing overlapping contributions from multiple mappings. To address this, points can be colored according to the index ii of the last applied WiWi​, revealing the partitioned structure of the attractor and the relative influence of each transformation in the union.[9]
Variations
Restricted Chaos Game
In the restricted chaos game, the standard algorithm is modified by imposing rules on vertex selection to prevent immediate repetition or selection of nearby vertices, thereby reducing clustering and altering the density of the generated fractal. After selecting a vertex ViVi​, the next vertex is chosen randomly from the remaining options, excluding ViVi​ itself or, in more stringent variants, the most recent mm selections, where mm is a small integer such as 1 or 2. This modification maintains a "memory" of the last mm vertices and samples uniformly from the n−mn−m available vertices, where nn is the total number of vertices in the initial polygon. The primary effect of these restrictions is to produce fractals with smoother boundaries and more even filling of interior regions, as the avoidance of local repeats distributes points more uniformly across the attractor compared to the unrestricted version. This approach is particularly useful for generating curve-like fractals such as the dragon curve or Lévy C curve, where the restrictions help trace space-filling paths without excessive overlap.
Non-Contractive Expansions (r > 1)
In the chaos game, when the contraction ratio rr exceeds 1, the affine transformations become expansive rather than contractive, leading to mappings that increase distances between points. This shift results in orbits that generally diverge from the initial position, producing unbounded trajectories unless additional constraints, such as probabilistic selection or spatial bounding, are imposed to maintain visualization. The core update rule for point generation remains Pk=(1−r)Pk−1+rViPk​=(1−r)Pk−1​+rVi​, where ViVi​ is a randomly selected vertex from the defining set, but with r>1r>1, the term rVirVi​ amplifies deviations from Pk−1Pk−1​, causing exponential growth in the point positions over iterations. Stability analysis of the fixed points in this linear system reveals instability when ∣1−r∣>1∣1−r∣>1, which holds for r>2r>2 (since 1−r<−11−r<−1), leading to rapid divergence; for 1<r<21<r<2, the dynamics exhibit slower expansion or potential oscillations before escaping bounded regions. These expansive dynamics generate unbounded fractal-like structures, often filling the plane densely, but practical visualization requires normalization techniques, such as projecting points into a unit square via transformations like (x,y)↦(x1+∣x∣,y1+∣y∣)(x,y)↦(1+∣x∣x​,1+∣y∣y​), which maps diverging orbits to a bounded domain while preserving the fractal density. The resulting images can resemble filled Julia sets, highlighting the method's utility in exploring repeller structures. Applications of non-contractive expansions extend to modeling chaotic attractors in dynamical systems exhibiting expansive behavior, where traditional contractive IFS fail to capture diverging orbits. Furthermore, this framework connects to inverse iterated function systems (IFS), in which the expansive forward mappings of a repeller become contractive inverses; applying the chaos game to these inverses generates the repeller as an attractor, as seen in constructions of Julia sets via modified inverse iteration methods.
Alternative Jump Sizes
In the chaos game, alternative jump sizes refer to variations in the contraction ratio rr (where 0<r<10<r<1 and r≠1/2r=1/2), which determines the fraction of the distance moved toward a randomly selected vertex at each iteration. Unlike the standard r=1/2r=1/2, which produces non-overlapping, touching substructures in many iterated function systems (IFS), smaller values like r=1/3r=1/3 result in finer substructures with gaps between scaled copies, requiring more iterations to approximate the attractor and yielding sparser, disconnected components. Conversely, larger values such as r=2/3r=2/3 lead to coarser approximations, where substructures overlap, creating denser patterns with reduced fine-scale detail but faster convergence to a filled-like appearance.[18] These non-standard jump sizes distort the self-similarity of the generated fractal, as the spatial arrangement of iterated points no longer aligns perfectly with the IFS maps designed for r=1/2r=1/2. For instance, in a triangular IFS, r=1/3r=1/3 produces a Sierpinski-like gasket that is disconnected, with three isolated smaller triangles separated by empty space, emphasizing finer hierarchical levels but lowering overall density. Parameter sweeps visualizing rr from 0.1 to 0.9 reveal a transition: low rr yields fragmented, intricate patterns; intermediate rr near 0.5 restores balanced self-similarity; and high rr causes progressive overlap, blurring boundaries. A notable example involves pentagonal IFS, where r=1/ϕ≈0.618r=1/ϕ≈0.618 (the inverse of the golden ratio ϕ=(1+5)/2ϕ=(1+5
​)/2) exploits the pentagon's geometric symmetry to generate a fractal with interconnected, star-like substructures, linking the chaos game to properties of regular pentagons.[18] The impact on fractal morphology is quantifiable through the Hausdorff dimension dd, which for an IFS with nn equal-probability contractions of ratio rr satisfies the equation
nrd=1  ⟹  d=log⁡nlog⁡(1/r).
nrd=1⟹d=log(1/r)logn​. This adjustment for non-standard rr alters dd relative to the canonical case; for the triangular example, r=1/3r=1/3 gives d=1d=1 (a curve-like set), while r=2/3r=2/3 yields d≈2.71d≈2.71 (denser than the standard ≈1.58≈1.58). For the pentagonal case with r=1/ϕr=1/ϕ, d≈3.35d≈3.35, exceeding the plane's embedding dimension and indicating significant overlaps that enrich the structure. These variations highlight how jump sizes tune the balance between detail and coherence in chaos game outputs.[19]
Advanced Applications
Optimal r for Regular Polygons
In the context of the chaos game applied to regular n-sided polygons, the optimal contraction ratio roptropt​ is defined as the value that ensures the first-level self-similar regions— the images of the polygon under the contraction maps fi(P)=(1−r)P+rvifi​(P)=(1−r)P+rvi​—touch at boundaries without overlapping interiors, thereby minimizing visual artifacts such as gaps or dense clusters in finite iterations.[20] This optimization is particularly relevant for generating approximations of polygonal structures, where for n=3n=3, it recovers the Sierpinski gasket, while for n≥4n≥4, the attractor is the entire filled polygon with uniform point density achieved across it in the limit, though roptropt​ aids faster convergence to uniformity. The derivation of roptropt​ relies on the geometry of the regular n-gon, assuming unit edge length ℓ=1ℓ=1 for simplicity. It is given by ropt=δ∥δ∥+1ropt​=δ∥​+1δ∥​​, where δ∥δ∥​ is the maximum span of the vertex projections onto the direction parallel to any edge, computed as δ∥=2max⁡k=0n−1sin⁡((2k−1)πn)/(2sin⁡(πn))δ∥​=2maxk=0n−1​sin(n(2k−1)π​)/(2sin(nπ​)). This formula balances the contraction such that the first-level images touch but do not overlap, verified through simulations measuring overlap via Hausdorff distance.[20] For n≥4n≥4, higher iterations fill the polygon densely, resulting in a uniform distribution rather than a sparse fractal. Sequence Representation
In the chaos game, sequences such as DNA or binary strings can be represented by mapping each symbol to a specific vertex selection, where the iterative plotting of points encodes the sequential information into a fractal trajectory on the attractor. This approach, known as Chaos Game Representation (CGR), transforms a one-dimensional sequence into a two-dimensional graphical form by applying the game's transformations deterministically based on the sequence symbols rather than random choices. For instance, in DNA sequences, the nucleotides A, C, G, and T are assigned to the four vertices of a square, and each successive symbol dictates the vertex toward which the current point moves by a fixed fraction (typically 1/2) of the distance. Applications of this representation are prominent in bioinformatics, where CGR visualizes genomic sequences by plotting trajectories that highlight structural features like periodicity or repeats in DNA. For binary sequences, the method maps 0 and 1 to the endpoints of an interval, generating paths that approximate the middle-thirds Cantor set, a fractal with measure zero but uncountable points, allowing the encoding of binary data into a self-similar structure. This deterministic use of sequences has been extended to protein sequences and other symbolic data, facilitating tasks such as similarity detection without explicit alignment.[21][22] The advantages of CGR include its ability to reveal hidden patterns or periodicity within the sequence through the density and clustering of points on the attractor, providing an intuitive visual map of local and global structures that linear representations obscure. In bioinformatics, it supports sequence alignment and comparison by quantifying similarities via image-based metrics, such as correlation coefficients between CGR plots, which correlate with biological relatedness. Additionally, frequency-based variants like Frequency Chaos Game Representation (FCGR) convert sequences into matrices that capture motif frequencies, enabling machine learning applications for classification and anomaly detection.[23][24] A representative example involves a binary string applied to the Cantor set: starting from an initial point in [0,1], each bit selects a transformation—0 maps to multiplication by 1/3 (left subinterval), and 1 maps to (x + 2)/3 (right subinterval)—producing a trajectory that converges to a point in the set determined by the infinite sequence. For a periodic binary string like alternating 0s and 1s (010101...), the path oscillates between subintervals, densely filling segments of the attractor and approximating its self-similar structure; density plots of such representations can then illustrate motif frequencies, such as the prevalence of runs of identical bits, by highlighting brighter regions corresponding to repeated subsequences.[21][24]
